title: What is Delta Lake: an open-source storage layer on top of Parquet that brings ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and DML (UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE) to a data lake: and how does it differ from plain Parquet (transaction log, concurrent writes, schema evolution)?
shortTitle: What is Delta Lake and how it differs from plain Parquet
keyPoints: Delta Lake is Parquet plus a transaction log (_delta_log) that turns a folder of files into an ACID table.
Each commit is an atomic set of actions (add/remove files) recorded as a numbered JSON file in the log.
Readers reconstruct the table at version N by replaying commits 0 through N.
Optimistic concurrency control handles concurrent writers: only one can create the next log entry.
Schema enforcement rejects writes with wrong columns or types; schema evolution is opt-in with mergeSchema.
Time travel lets you query any prior version with versionAsOf or timestampAsOf.
VACUUM removes old files after a retention period, freeing storage used by time travel.

s1_definition.oneliner: Delta Lake is Parquet plus a transaction log that turns a dumb folder of files into an ACID, versioned, updatable table.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Delta Lake** – an open-source storage layer on top of Parquet that adds transactional capabilities to a data lake.
- **Transaction log (_delta_log)** – an ordered directory of JSON commit files plus periodic Parquet checkpoints that records every change to the table.
- **ACID transactions** – atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability provided by the commit protocol.
- **Schema enforcement** – rejecting writes whose columns or types do not match the table definition.
- **Time travel** – querying the table as it was at a previous version or timestamp.
- **MERGE** – an atomic DML operation that inserts new rows and updates existing ones in one step.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps all its transaction records as plain Parquet files in a folder. If Rajesh's transfer writes new files while a report is being generated, the report might read half-written data: there is no referee. Delta Lake adds a strict ledger (the transaction log) that records "at version 5, these files are the truth." Everyone reads the ledger first, so nobody ever sees a half-finished write, and you can ask "show me the table as it was at version 3 this morning."

sections.s2_detail:
### What is wrong with plain Parquet?

Plain Parquet is just a columnar file format. A "Parquet table" is really a directory of .parquet files with no coordinator. When a writer adds or rewrites files, a concurrent reader can see a partial result, there is no way to atomically replace data, and there is no history.

```java
package com.bank.formats;

public class PlainParquetProblems {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Plain Parquet problems:");
        System.out.println("  1. No ACID: concurrent reader sees"
            + " half-written files");
        System.out.println("  2. No atomic replace: partial update"
            + " visible");
        System.out.println("  3. No history: cannot query old versions");
        System.out.println("  4. No UPDATE/DELETE: must rewrite"
            + " entire dataset");
        System.out.println("  5. No schema enforcement: bad columns"
            + " land silently");
    }
}
```

```text
Plain Parquet problems:
  1. No ACID: concurrent reader sees half-written files
  2. No atomic replace: partial update visible
  3. No history: cannot query old versions
  4. No UPDATE/DELETE: must rewrite entire dataset
  5. No schema enforcement: bad columns land silently
```

### How does the Delta transaction log work?

Delta Lake adds the `_delta_log` folder containing numbered JSON commit files. Each commit is an atomic set of actions: `add` (new data file), `remove` (file logically deleted), and `metaData` (schema or partitioning changed). Readers reconstruct the table at version N by replaying commits 0 through N.

```text
s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta/
  _delta_log/
    00000000000000000000.json   (version 0: initial load)
    00000000000000000001.json   (version 1: append)
    00000000000000000002.json   (version 2: merge/update)
    00000000000000000003.json   (version 3: delete)
    00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet (checkpoint)
  part-00000-abc123.parquet
  part-00001-def456.parquet
  part-00002-ghi789.parquet
```

```java
package com.bank.formats;

public class DeltaLogExplained {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Commit 0: add part-00000, part-00001");
        System.out.println("Commit 1: add part-00002");
        System.out.println("Commit 2: remove part-00000,"
            + " add part-00003");
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("Table at version 2:");
        System.out.println("  Active files: part-00001, part-00002,"
            + " part-00003");
        System.out.println("  Removed: part-00000 (old, for time travel)");
    }
}
```

```text
Commit 0: add part-00000, part-00001
Commit 1: add part-00002
Commit 2: remove part-00000, add part-00003

Table at version 2:
  Active files: part-00001, part-00002, part-00003
  Removed: part-00000 (old, for time travel)
```

### How does ACID work in Delta Lake?

Because each commit is a single atomic file creation, either the whole change is visible or none of it is. Concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency control: two writers prepare commits, race to create the next numbered log entry, and only one succeeds. The loser retries.

```python
# Atomic append: either the whole commit is visible or not
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(
    "s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")

# If two writers race:
#   Writer A creates 00000003.json -> succeeds
#   Writer B tries 00000003.json -> fails (exists)
#   Writer B re-reads state, retries as 00000004.json
```

```java
package com.bank.formats;

public class DeltaACID {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("ACID properties in Delta Lake:");
        System.out.println("  Atomicity: commit is one file creation");
        System.out.println("  Consistency: schema enforced per write");
        System.out.println("  Isolation: readers see committed versions");
        System.out.println("  Durability: log and data on S3/HDFS");
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("Concurrency: optimistic locking");
        System.out.println("  Race -> one wins, loser retries.");
    }
}
```

```text
ACID properties in Delta Lake:
  Atomicity: commit is one file creation
  Consistency: schema enforced per write
  Isolation: readers see committed versions
  Durability: log and data on S3/HDFS

Concurrency: optimistic locking
  Race -> one wins, loser retries.
```

### How does schema enforcement and evolution work?

Schema enforcement rejects writes whose columns or types do not match the table, protecting against silent data corruption. Schema evolution is opt-in with `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`, which safely adds new columns.

```python
# Schema enforcement: rejects mismatched write
df_bad = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("T1", "extra_col_value")], ["txn_id", "unknown_col"])
try:
    df_bad.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(
        "s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")
except Exception as e:
    print("Rejected:", e)
# AnalysisException: schema mismatch

# Schema evolution: add new column safely
df_new.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("append") \
    .option("mergeSchema", "true") \
    .save("s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")
```

### How does time travel work?

Time travel lets you query the table as it was at any prior version or timestamp. Old files remain after updates until VACUUM removes them.

```python
# Time travel by version
df_v3 = spark.read.format("delta") \
    .option("versionAsOf", 3) \
    .load("s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")

# Time travel by timestamp
df_yesterday = spark.read.format("delta") \
    .option("timestampAsOf", "2024-10-28") \
    .load("s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")

# Audit: what did the table look like before the correction?
df_yesterday.show(5)
```

```java
package com.bank.formats;

public class TimeTravel {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Time travel use cases:");
        System.out.println("  1. Audit: table before a correction job");
        System.out.println("  2. Debug: compare before/after a bug");
        System.out.println("  3. ML: reproducible training snapshots");
        System.out.println("  4. Compliance: prove historical state");
    }
}
```

```text
Time travel use cases:
  1. Audit: table before a correction job
  2. Debug: compare before/after a bug
  3. ML: reproducible training snapshots
  4. Compliance: prove historical state
```

### How do UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE work?

Delta does not mutate Parquet files in place. UPDATE and DELETE rewrite only the files containing matching rows and record the swap in the log. MERGE combines insert and update in one atomic operation.

```python
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

delta = DeltaTable.forPath(spark,
    "s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")

# DELETE cancelled transactions
delta.delete("status = 'CANCELLED'")

# UPDATE a correction
delta.update(
    condition="txn_id = 'T10045'",
    set={"amount": "16000.00"})

# MERGE: upsert new and updated records
delta.alias("t").merge(
    updates.alias("u"), "t.txn_id = u.txn_id"
).whenMatchedUpdateAll() \
 .whenNotMatchedInsertAll() \
 .execute()
```

### What is VACUUM?

VACUUM removes old files that are no longer referenced by any recent version, freeing storage. You must set a retention period; the default is 7 days to allow time-travel queries.

```python
# VACUUM: remove files older than 7 days
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
delta = DeltaTable.forPath(spark,
    "s3://bank-lake/curated/txns_delta")
delta.vacuum(168)  # 168 hours = 7 days
```

```java
package com.bank.formats;

public class VacuumExplained {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("VACUUM removes old unreferenced files.");
        System.out.println("  Retention: 7 days (default)");
        System.out.println("  After vacuum: time travel limited"
            + " to retention window.");
        System.out.println("  Run periodically to control storage cost.");
    }
}
```

```text
VACUUM removes old unreferenced files.
  Retention: 7 days (default)
  After vacuum: time travel limited to retention window.
  Run periodically to control storage cost.
```

### What are common interview follow-up questions?

- How does Delta Lake compare to Apache Iceberg and Hudi?
- What is optimistic concurrency control and when does it conflict?
- How does MERGE rewrite only the affected files?
- What is the role of checkpoint files in the transaction log?
- How do you handle Delta Lake compaction (OPTIMIZE)?
sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Plain Parquet vs Delta Lake
  ───────────────────────────

  Plain Parquet (no coordinator)       Delta Lake (transaction log)
  ┌──────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ part-00000.parquet   │             │ _delta_log/              │
  │ part-00001.parquet   │             │   0000.json (v0: add)    │
  │ part-00002.parquet   │             │   0001.json (v1: add)    │
  │                      │             │   0002.json (v2: merge)  │
  │ No ACID              │             │                          │
  │ No history           │             │ part-00000.parquet       │
  │ No schema check      │             │ part-00001.parquet       │
  │ Concurrent read/write│             │ part-00002.parquet       │
  │ = partial result     │             │                          │
  └──────────────────────┘             │ ACID, time travel,       │
                                       │ schema enforcement       │
                                       └──────────────────────────┘
```

```text
  MERGE Operation
  ───────────────
  Before:                After:
  ┌──────────┐           ┌──────────┐
  │ part-001 │           │ part-001 │ (unchanged: no match)
  │ part-002 │ ─rewrite─▶│ part-004 │ (rewritten: matches updated)
  │ part-003 │           │ part-003 │ (unchanged)
  └──────────┘           │ part-005 │ (new: inserts)
                         └──────────┘
  Log: remove part-002, add part-004, add part-005
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Delta Lake is an open-source storage layer that sits on top of Parquet files and adds a transaction log to turn a plain folder of files into a real table with ACID guarantees. Plain Parquet is only a file format with no coordinator, so concurrent writes can be seen half-finished, there is no atomic replace, and there is no history. Delta solves all three because every change is committed as one atomic log entry, and readers reconstruct a consistent snapshot by replaying the log.

Delta gives four things Parquet cannot. ACID transactions through optimistic concurrency control. Schema enforcement that rejects mismatched writes, with evolution available via mergeSchema. Time travel to query any prior version. And row-level DML: UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE that rewrite only affected files and record the swap in the log. VACUUM removes old files after a retention period to control storage.

In a banking context at the National Bank of India, the nightly job appended transactions to a Delta table while analysts ran reports, and because readers only see committed versions, a report never picked up half-written files. When a compliance officer asked what a table looked like before a correction, time travel answered the question. And when a bad upstream feed tried to add an unexpected column, schema enforcement rejected it.

The way to summarize it in interviews is that Delta is Parquet plus a transaction log, and that log is the difference between a dumb pile of files and a trustworthy, versioned, updatable banking table.

Remember one sentence: Delta Lake is Parquet plus a transaction log that provides ACID, schema enforcement, time travel, and DML on a data lake.
